clinicalPearls: Staphylococcus aureus, streptococci, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are the most common causes of infectious arthritis, though mycobacteria, spirochetes, fungi, and viruses can also seed joints.
Acute bacterial infection can rapidly destroy articular cartilage, so every inflamed joint warrants prompt evaluation; cartilage degradation can begin within about 48 hours.
Roughly 90% of acute septic arthritis presents in a single joint, most often the knee, then the hip, and less often shoulder, wrist, or elbow.
In IV drug users, infections of the spine, sacroiliac joints, and sternoclavicular joints are more common than those of the appendicular skeleton.

Acute bacterial infection typically causes mono- or oligoarthritis; subacute/chronic monoarthritis suggests mycobacterial or fungal disease, and acute polyarthritis suggests viral, immunologic (endocarditis, rheumatic fever, DGI), or underlying rheumatoid disease.

Synovial fluid Gram stain is positive in roughly 30-50% of cases overall; organisms are seen on smear in nearly three-quarters of S. aureus and streptococcal infections but only 30-50% of gram-negative and other bacterial infections.

Synovial fluid cultures are positive in over 90% of nongonococcal bacterial arthritis cases, but in gonococcal arthritis synovial cultures are frequently negative and blood cultures positive in fewer than 45%.

Disseminated gonococcal infection most commonly presents as an arthritis-dermatitis syndrome with fever, chills, hemorrhagic pustular rash, tenosynovitis, and migratory arthritis; women are 2-3 times more likely than men to develop DGI, with peak risk during menses and pregnancy.

Lyme disease causes arthritis in up to 60% of untreated persons; serologic IgG to B. burgdorferi is positive in over 90% of Lyme arthritis, and NAAT detects Borrelia DNA in synovial fluid in about 85%.

Tuberculous arthritis is usually a chronic granulomatous monoarthritis of large weight-bearing joints (hips, knees, ankles); synovial fluid acid-fast staining is positive in under one-third of cases but synovial tissue culture is positive in about 90%.

Parvovirus B19 causes polyarthritis or polyarthralgia in about 60% of infected women and 10% of children; rubella, mumps, hepatitis B, and arboviruses (Zika, chikungunya, Ross River) are other notable viral causes.

Prosthetic joint infection complicates roughly 0.5-2% of total joint replacements and is more common after knee than hip arthroplasty; indolent infection with coagulase-negative staphylococci, Cutibacterium, enterococci, or diphtheroids may persist for months to years without constitutional symptoms.
harrison.pathophysiology: Bacteria reach the joint hematogenously, from a contiguous bone or soft-tissue focus, or by direct inoculation during surgery, injection, bite, or trauma. In hematogenous infection, organisms escape from synovial capillaries, which lack a limiting basement membrane, and within hours provoke neutrophilic infiltration of the synovium. Neutrophils and bacteria enter the joint space and bacteria adhere to articular cartilage. Cartilage degradation begins within about 48 hours owing to increased intraarticular pressure, release of proteases and cytokines from chondrocytes and synovial macrophages, and invasion of cartilage by bacteria and inflammatory cells. Synovial proliferation forms a pannus over the cartilage, and thrombosis of inflamed synovial vessels develops; abscesses may extend into synovium, cartilage, and subchondral bone. S. aureus surface adhesins promote cartilage adherence and endotoxins drive chondrocyte-mediated cartilage breakdown. Gonococcal arthritis-dermatitis and viral arthritides are believed to be largely immune-mediated, reflecting reaction to circulating organisms and immune-complex deposition rather than direct joint invasion.
additionalDifferentials: Crystal-induced arthritis (gout, pseudogout) - can clinically mimic and may coexist with septic arthritis
infectionMimics: Gonococcal disseminated infection presenting as arthritis-dermatitis (versus true septic monoarthritis)
Meningococcemia with dermatitis-arthritis or purulent monoarthritis
Poncet's disease (reactive polyarthritis of disseminated tuberculosis, with no organisms in the joint)
Viral arthritides (parvovirus B19, rubella, hepatitis B, arboviruses)
Postinfectious/reactive arthritis following enteric or chlamydial infection
additionalInvestigations: Arthrocentesis with synovial fluid cell count, differential, Gram stain, and culture (obtain before antibiotics)
Synovial fluid examination for crystals to exclude/identify coexistent gout or pseudogout
Blood cultures (positive in up to 50-70% of S. aureus infections)
Inoculation of synovial fluid into blood-culture bottles to improve yield for fastidious organisms
Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT) and MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry for partially treated or culture-negative cases
Sonication of explanted prosthetic material to disrupt biofilm and improve culture yield
Plain radiographs; ultrasound for hip effusion; CT/MRI for sacroiliac, sternoclavicular, and spinal joint infection
Mucosal cultures (endocervical/urethral, rectal, oropharyngeal) and urine NAAT when gonococcal arthritis is suspected
Synovial tissue biopsy and culture for suspected mycobacterial or fungal arthritis
redFlags: Acutely inflamed joint - treat as a medical emergency given rapid cartilage destruction
Narrowing of joint space and bony erosions on radiographs indicate advanced infection and poor prognosis
Septic arthritis of the hip, especially in young children, threatens viability of the femoral head and is best managed surgically
Polyarticular involvement or absent fever in rheumatoid, renal, hepatic, or immunosuppressed patients can mask infection
Failure of repeated needle aspiration to clear effusion, lower synovial WBC, and sterilize cultures signals need for arthroscopic or open drainage
harrison.prognosis: Prompt systemic antibiotics with timely joint drainage can prevent cartilage destruction, postinfectious degenerative arthritis, joint instability, and deformity, so outcome depends heavily on early recognition and adequate decompression. Radiographic joint-space narrowing and bony erosions indicate advanced disease and a poorer outcome. Gonococcal and Lyme arthritis generally respond well to therapy, and most reactive arthritis resolves within about 6 months, though recurrent disease is more common after chlamydial urethritis. Untreated Lyme arthritis leaves about 10% with chronic erosive synovitis, and certain viral arthropathies (e.g., parvovirus B19) occasionally become chronic.
pitfalls: Serum procalcitonin is only about 50% sensitive and must not be used to rule out infectious arthritis.
Elevated synovial protein and lactate dehydrogenase with depressed glucose are nonspecific and not required for diagnosis.
Failing to test synovial fluid for crystals can miss coexisting infection and crystal disease, which can occur together.
Relying on synovial fluid culture in suspected gonococcal arthritis is misleading, since cultures are often negative; mucosal-site cultures and NAAT are needed.

Coagulase-negative staphylococci, Cutibacterium, or diphtheroids in a prosthetic joint may represent indolent true infection rather than contamination, so semiquantitative culture and careful aspiration technique are important.
Cellulitis, bursitis, and osteomyelitis can mimic septic arthritis; preserved passive range of motion and less-than-circumferential swelling help distinguish them.
Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) are typically elevated but nonspecific.
harrison.severityClassification: No single formal grading system; synovial fluid cell count guides likelihood and severity. Normal synovial fluid contains fewer than 180 cells/uL (predominantly mononuclear). Acute bacterial infection averages about 100,000 cells/uL (range roughly 25,000-250,000/uL) with over 90% neutrophils. Crystal-induced, rheumatoid, and other noninfectious inflammatory arthritides usually show under 30,000-50,000 cells/uL. Mycobacterial and fungal infections typically show 10,000-30,000 cells/uL with 50-70% neutrophils. Gonococcal DGI synovial fluid usually contains only 10,000-20,000 leukocytes/uL, whereas true gonococcal septic arthritis contains over 50,000/uL.
